claim: Humans have the ability to learn new visual concepts from just a single exemplar.
source: Humans have the amazing ability to learn new visual concepts from just a single exemplar.
evidence: This is a foundational claim stated in the abstract and supported throughout the manuscript by experimental results.

claim: State-of-the-art theories suggest observers rely on internal 'generative models' for one-shot learning.
source: State-of-the-art theories suggest observers rely on internal 'generative models', which not only describe observed objects, but can also synthesize novel variations.
evidence: This claim references theoretical frameworks in the field, supported by citations throughout the introduction.

claim: Compelling evidence for generative models in human one-shot learning remains sparse.
source: However, compelling evidence for generative models in human one-shot learning remains sparse.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: In most studies, participants merely compare candidate objects created by experimenters rather than generating their own ideas.
source: In most studies, participants merely compare candidate objects created by the experimenters, rather than generating their own ideas.
evidence: This describes a limitation of previous experimental approaches, based on review of the literature.

claim: Participants inferred and synthesized genuine novel categories that were far more varied than mere copies.
source: The drawings reveal that participants inferred—and synthesized—genuine novel categories that were far more varied than mere copies.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from Experiments 1 and 2b.

claim: There was striking agreement between participants about which shape features were most distinctive.
source: Yet, there was striking agreement between participants about which shape features were most distinctive, and these tended to be preserved in the drawn Variations.
evidence: This finding is supported by data from Experiment 5 showing high inter-observer agreement.

claim: Distinctive parts tended to be preserved in the drawn Variations.
source: Yet, there was striking agreement between participants about which shape features were most distinctive, and these tended to be preserved in the drawn Variations.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiments 4 and 5 showing correspondence and preservation of distinctive features.

claim: Swapping distinctive parts caused objects to swap apparent category.
source: Indeed, swapping distinctive parts caused objects to swap apparent category.
evidence: This is a key finding from Experiment 6 demonstrating the causal role of distinctive parts.

claim: Internal generative models are key to how humans generalize from single exemplars.
source: Our findings suggest that internal generative models are key to how humans generalize from single exemplars.
evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: When observers see a novel object for the first time, they identify its most distinctive features and infer a generative model of its shape.
source: When observers see a novel object for the first time, they identify its most distinctive features and infer a generative model of its shape, allowing them to mentally synthesize plausible variants.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by the pattern of results across all experiments.

claim: Humans can rapidly classify objects (Thorpe et al., 1996; Mack and Palmeri, 2015; Serre et al., 2007).
source: Humans can rapidly classify objects (Thorpe et al., 1996; Mack and Palmeri, 2015; Serre et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Humans can rapidly classify complex scenes (Wilder et al., 2018; Fei-Fei et al., 2007).
source: complex scenes (Wilder et al., 2018; Fei-Fei et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Humans can rapidly classify materials (Sharan et al., 2010) into familiar classes.
source: and materials (Sharan et al., 2010) into familiar classes
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Humans can build new classes when presented with sufficient examples (Op de Beeck and Baker, 2010; Gauthier et al., 1998).
source: as well as build new classes when presented with sufficient examples (Op de Beeck and Baker, 2010; Gauthier et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Computational models trained with large training sets can emulate many human abilities in pattern recognition and categorization (Huang et al., 2017; Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Szegedy et al., 2017; Szegedy et al., 2015; Szegedy et al., 2016; He et al., 2016; Radford, 2021; Kubilius et al., 2016; Jozwik et al., 2018; Jozwik et al., 2016; Jozwik et al., 2019).
source: When large numbers of examples are provided, the mathematical basis of human pattern recognition and categorization is well described, and computational models trained with large training sets can emulate many of the human abilities in these areas (Huang et al., 2017; Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Szegedy et al., 2017; Szegedy et al., 2015; Szegedy et al., 2016; He et al., 2016; Radford, 2021; Kubilius et al., 2016; Jozwik et al., 2018; Jozwik et al., 2016; Jozwik et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to machine learning literature.

claim: Humans have the ability to infer new classes when presented with only a small number or even just one single example (Feldman, 1992; Feldman, 1997; Ons and Wagemans, 2012; Richards et al., 1992; Morgenstern et al., 2019; Ayzenberg and Lourenco, 2021).
source: However, humans also have the amazing ability to infer new classes when presented with only a small number or even just one single example, as typically occurs when first encountering new concepts ('one-shot categorization'; Feldman, 1992; Feldman, 1997; Ons and Wagemans, 2012; Richards et al., 1992; Morgenstern et al., 2019; Ayzenberg and Lourenco, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on one-shot learning.

claim: One-shot learning is crucial to the formation of human perceptual categories, particularly at early stages of visual development (Gelman and Markman, 1986; Gelman and Meyer, 2011; Gopnik and Sobel, 2000; Smith and Slone, 2017; Yuan et al., 2020; Gershkoff-Stowe et al., 1997; Landau et al., 1988; Landau et al., 1998; Pereira and Smith, 2009).
source: Such one-shot learning—which we here use interchangeably with one-shot categorization—is crucial to the formation of human perceptual categories, particularly at early stages of visual development (Gelman and Markman, 1986; Gelman and Meyer, 2011; Gopnik and Sobel, 2000; Smith and Slone, 2017; Yuan et al., 2020; Gershkoff-Stowe et al., 1997; Landau et al., 1988; Landau et al., 1998; Pereira and Smith, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to developmental psychology research.

claim: One-shot learning is a significant challenge for artificial learning systems (Geirhos et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021; Baker et al., 2018; Michaelis et al., 2020).
source: Yet how we achieve this remains mysterious and is a significant challenge for artificial learning systems (Geirhos et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021; Baker et al., 2018; Michaelis et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to machine learning literature.

claim: Given only a single exemplar of a category, there is an infinite number of sets containing that exemplar, any of which could in principle be the true category from which the exemplar was drawn.
source: Given only a single exemplar of a category, there is an infinite number of sets containing that exemplar, any of which could in principle be the true category from which the exemplar was drawn.
evidence: This is a logical statement about the computational problem of one-shot learning.

claim: State-of-the-art approaches in psychology and computer science suggest that humans infer a generative model which considers the observed exemplar as a single sample from a statistical generative process (Feldman, 1992; Feldman, 1997; Fei-Fei et al., 2006; Goodman et al., 2008a; Goodman et al., 2008b; Lake et al., 2015; Stuhlmuller et al., 2010).
source: The state-of-the-art in psychology and computer science for understanding how humans generalize from few samples suggest that they infer a generative model, which considers the observed exemplar as a single sample from a statistical generative process (Feldman, 1992; Feldman, 1997; Fei-Fei et al., 2006; Goodman et al., 2008a; Goodman et al., 2008b; Lake et al., 2015; Stuhlmuller et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and computational work.

claim: Observers have a 'deep' understanding of objects, such that they infer the causes or processes that generated the object (Fleming and Schmidt, 2019; Schmidt et al., 2019).
source: In intuitive terms, it is assumed that observers have a 'deep' understanding of objects, such that they infer the causes or processes that generated the object (Fleming and Schmidt, 2019; Schmidt et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Generative models can be used to identify behaviourally significant features to judge new samples and can also be used to synthesize or imagine new objects from the same class.
source: Importantly, generative models can not only be used to identify behaviourally significant features to judge new samples but can also be used to synthesize or imagine new (i.e., never observed) objects from the same class.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the properties of generative models.

claim: A key step in the inference of a generative model is the identification of diagnostic features that are informative about the underlying generative processes and therefore category membership.
source: A key step in the inference of a generative model for a given exemplar is the identification of diagnostic features that are informative about the underlying generative processes and therefore category membership.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about how generative models work.

claim: Differentiating between generic and non-generic diagnostic features, such as particular relationships between elements in objects (e.g., symmetry) is one important cue to underlying generative processes (Feldman, 1997).
source: Differentiating between these generic and non-generic (or 'non-transverse'), diagnostic features, such as particular relationships between elements in objects (e.g., symmetry) is one important cue to underlying generative processes (Feldman, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Feldman's theoretical work.

claim: Cue features might include statistical outliers in the shape (e.g., a sharp protrusion, or an angle), that makes a local feature stand out within the shape (Feldman and Singh, 2005; Feldman and Singh, 2006; Feldman, 2013; Op de Beeck et al., 2008; Kayaert et al., 2005).
source: Other cue features might include statistical outliers in the shape (e.g., a sharp protrusion, or an angle), that makes a local feature stand out within the shape (Feldman and Singh, 2005; Feldman and Singh, 2006; Feldman, 2013; Op de Beeck et al., 2008; Kayaert et al., 2005), or compared to others seen previously.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on shape perception.

claim: Tasks exploring categorization and generalization typically ask observers to discriminate between multiple presented objects (Ashby and Maddox, 2005).
source: Typically, tasks exploring categorization and generalization ask observers to discriminate between multiple presented objects (Ashby and Maddox, 2005)
evidence: This describes typical experimental methods in the field, supported by citation.

claim: The process of presenting multiple objects potentially interferes with how observers perform categorization tasks.
source: Yet, the very process of presenting multiple objects potentially interferes with how observers perform the task.
evidence: This is a methodological critique based on logical reasoning about task demands.

claim: Observers can solve discrimination tasks simply by comparing how similar objects are to one another, without establishing preferences for particular features, and without synthesizing new variants.
source: Rather than using a generative model, observers can solve these types of discrimination tasks simply by comparing how similar objects are to one another, without establishing preferences for particular features, and without synthesizing new variants.
evidence: This is a logical claim about alternative strategies available in typical experimental paradigms.

claim: The experimenter determines the range of possible options observers can choose from in typical categorization experiments, thereby crucially constraining the range of responses.
source: Another key limitation is that the experimenter—rather than the observer—determines the range of possible options the observers can choose from, thereby crucially constraining the range of responses.
evidence: This is a methodological critique of typical experimental designs.

claim: Seventeen participants each drew 12 Variations for each of 8 Exemplars, yielding a total of 204 Variations per Exemplar (1632 drawings overall).
source: For each of the 8 Exemplars, 17 participants ('drawers') each drew 12 Variations (yielding a total of 204 Variations per Exemplar, i.e., 1632 drawings overall).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size of Experiment 1.

claim: Exemplars were created by combining a main body with varying numbers of parts (ranging from 0 to 5) and displaying a wide range of visual features.
source: Exemplars were created by the experimenters by combining a main body with varying numbers of parts (ranging from 0 to 5) and displaying a wide range of visual features, such as positive and negative parts (e.g., the indentation in Exemplar 2), curvatures (polygonal and curved shapes), and complexity of parts (e.g., the 'spike' in Exemplar 4 vs. the 'twirl' in Exemplar 6).
evidence: This describes the stimulus creation procedure.

claim: The aim of creating diverse Exemplars was to maximize generalizations as well as limit the impact of semantic knowledge.
source: The aim was to create Exemplars that are diverse without resembling real-world objects, to maximize generalizations as well as limit the impact of semantic knowledge.
evidence: This describes the rationale for stimulus design.

claim: Participants varied substantially in how much their drawings deviated from the Exemplar (creativity).
source: Figure 1d shows the average similarity of produced Variations for each participant, demonstrating that participants varied substantially in how much their drawings deviated from the Exemplar, that is, in their creativity when producing Variations.
evidence: This finding is shown in Figure 1d and described in the text.

claim: Age of drawing (whether a shape was drawn earlier or later within the sequence) did not predict similarity (R² < 0.01, F(1,10) = 0.08, p = 0.77).
source: Linear regression showed that age of drawing (i.e., whether a shape was drawn earlier or later within the sequence of 12 shapes for each Exemplar), did not predict similarity (R² < 0.01, F(1,10) = 0.08, p = 0.77).
evidence: This is a statistical result from linear regression analysis.

claim: In 95% of trials, copies were chosen over Variations when participants were asked to pick the shape that looked more like a copy of the Exemplar (chance = 50%).
source: In 95% of trials (chance = 50%) the copies were chosen, showing that the vast majority of a representative subset of Variations were perceived to be more different from the Exemplars than a mere copy (one-sided binomial test: 50%; N = 16,200, i.e., number of judgements; K (correct responses) = 15,388, p <0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2b showing that Variations are genuinely different from copies.

claim: The average percentage of correct classifications of Variations into their originating category was high (86%) and well above chance (12.5%).
source: The average percentage of correct classifications was high (86%) and well above chance (one-sided binomial test: 12.5%; N = 4800, i.e., number of judgements; K (correct responses) = 4111, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 3 showing that Variations form distinct perceptual categories.

claim: Almost all cells in the confusion matrix are significantly different from chance with all diagonal cells above and all others below chance.
source: Except for a single cell (row 4, column 1), all cells are significantly different from chance with all diagonal cells above—and all others below—chance (one-sided binomial tests with Bonferroni-adjusted p value of 0.015, according to the eight possible outcomes in each row).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 3 shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Performance in the three bins most similar to the Exemplars was virtually identical (overall 89%, 87%, and 88% correct responses).
source: Performance in the three bins most similar to the Exemplars was virtually identical (overall 89%, 87%, and 88% correct responses), with a maximum of 14% misclassifications in single cells.
evidence: This is a result from Experiment 3 analyzing performance as a function of similarity.

claim: For the least similar bin, performance dropped to 79%, suggesting that highly dissimilar shapes were significantly more often misclassified.
source: For the least similar bin, performance dropped to 79%, suggesting that highly dissimilar shapes were significantly more often misclassified, while overall classification accuracy was still way above chance.
evidence: This is a result from Experiment 3 showing the effect of similarity on categorization accuracy.

claim: Polygonal Exemplars tended to lead to polygonal Variations while curvaceous Exemplars led to curvaceous Variations (r = 0.99, p < 0.001).
source: We find that polygonal Exemplars tended to lead to polygonal Variations while curvaceous Exemplars led to curvaceous Variations (r = 0.99, p < 0.001; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing preservation of global curvature features, shown in Figure 2b.

claim: A pencil tracing a random walk is unlikely to draw a straight line, so straight lines are considered evidence of a significant (i.e., non-random) generative process.
source: This finding is broadly in line with the concept of non-random features indicating generative processes (Feldman, 1992; Feldman, 1997): A pencil tracing a random walk is unlikely to draw a straight line, so straight lines are considered evidence of a significant (i.e., non-random) generative process, which are therefore preserved in Variations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the curvature preservation finding in terms of Feldman's theory.

claim: On average, 71% of an Exemplar's area corresponded to some part of its Variations, with only 18% correspondence to Variations of other categories.
source: On average, 71% of an Exemplar's area corresponded to some part of its Variations, with only 18% correspondence to Variations of other categories (one-sided t-test: t(1199) = 38.84, p < 0.001, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 4 showing part correspondence within and across categories.

claim: The extent to which the Variation was seen to correspond was well predicted by similarity (R² = 0.92, F(1,8) = 96.69, p < 0.001).
source: We find that the extent to which the Variation was seen to correspond was well predicted by similarity (R² = 0.92, F(1,8) = 96.69, p < 0.001, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 4 showing the relationship between correspondence and similarity.

claim: A significant correlation exists between the percentage of correct categorizations and the percentage of corresponding area (r = 0.53, p < 0.01).
source: A significant correlation between the percentage of correct categorizations from Experiment 3 and the percentage of corresponding area (r = 0.53, p < 0.01) indicates that Variations that share more parts with the Exemplar are grouped more often with their Exemplar compared to those sharing fewer parts.
evidence: This is a statistical result showing the relationship between part correspondence and categorization accuracy.

claim: Out of the 80 Variations used in Experiment 4, 49 were always classified correctly, with a range in corresponding area between 30% and 100%, and a mean of 81%.
source: Notably, out of the 80 Variations used in Experiment 4, 49 were always classified correctly, with a range in corresponding area between 30% and 100%, and a mean of 81%.
evidence: This is a descriptive result from Experiments 3 and 4.

claim: Of trials with more than two correspondences, part order was identical in 77%, reversed in 7%, and shuffled in 17% of cases.
source: Of those trials with more than two correspondences, part order was identical in 77%, reversed in 7%, and shuffled in 17% of cases.
evidence: This is a result from the part order analysis of Experiment 4.

claim: Parts of the Exemplar were omitted in 4%, substituted with another non-corresponding part in 25%, or new parts were added that did not exist in the Exemplar in 8% of cases.
source: Analyzing gaps in part circles also provided a tentative measure of how often parts of the Exemplar were omitted (4%), substituted with another non-corresponding part (25%), or new parts were added that did not exist in the Exemplar (8%).
evidence: This is a result from the part change analysis of Experiment 4.

claim: More part substitutions occurred for less similar Variations to the Exemplar.
source: Notably, more part substitutions occurred for less similar Variations to the Exemplar (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: This is a result from the part change analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2d.

claim: The mean consecutive area of a shapes' silhouette with a high distinctiveness score (above 75% of the highest score) for the human data made up 19% of a shape's perimeter compared to <1% for the randomized data.
source: The mean consecutive area of a shapes' silhouette with a high distinctiveness score (above 75% of the highest score) for the human data made up 19% of a shape's perimeter compared to <1% for the randomized data (two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 5 showing high agreement about distinctive parts compared to chance.

claim: Comparing the distinctiveness scores of all Exemplar parts with the scores of all Variation parts of the same category shows a high correlation (r = 0.63; p < 0.001).
source: Comparing the scores of all Exemplar parts with the scores of all Variation parts of the same category shows a high correlation (r = 0.63; p < 0.001), suggesting that distinctive parts remain distinctive even when modified or shuffled within the overall part structure.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiments 4 and 5 showing preservation of distinctiveness.

claim: The proportion of correct responses from Experiment 2 (86%) was significantly higher than both swap conditions (69% for indistinctive swap, p < 0.001, and 32% for distinctive swap, p < 0.001).
source: Binomial tests indicate that the proportion of correct responses from Experiment 2 (86%) was significantly higher than both swap conditions (69% for indistinctive swap, p < 0.001, and 32% for distinctive swap, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 6 shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Swapping an indistinctive part has a small effect (Cohen's h = 0.29), while swapping a distinctive part has an immense effect on correct categorizations (Cohen's h = 1.05).
source: Further, we find a large difference in effect sizes: while swapping an indistinctive part does have a small effect (Cohen's h = 0.29), swapping a distinctive part has an immense effect on correct categorizations (Cohen's h = 1.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 6 showing the differential impact of distinctive vs. indistinctive parts.

claim: Most distinctive parts strongly biased participant's responses toward their categories, while only one indistinctive part had a significantly positive impact on its category choice.
source: Performing one-sided binomial tests on each of swapped-part conditions (with a Bonferroni-adjusted p level for 16 tests) shows that most distinctive parts strongly biased participant's responses toward their categories. In contrast, only one indistinctive part had a significantly positive impact on its category choice, while most indistinctive parts resulted in choices of their category even significantly below chance.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 6 shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Previous studies showed that small-to-intermediate fragments of an image are sufficient for correct categorization (Hegdé et al., 2008; Ullman et al., 2002).
source: Previous studies showed that small-to-intermediate fragments of an image are sufficient for correct categorization (Hegdé et al., 2008; Ullman et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Informative fragments in previous studies were defined by implicit analysis of the statistical distribution of features across the complete object category or categories.
source: These informative fragments were defined by implicit analysis of the statistical distribution of features across the complete object category or categories (i.e., the fragments were learned during a training phase).
evidence: This describes the methodology of previous studies cited.

claim: In the current experiments, parts were identified as distinctive from just a single piece of data (i.e., one object), consistently across many observers.
source: In contrast, in our experiments, parts were identified as distinctive from just a single piece of data (i.e., one object), consistently across many observers.
evidence: This contrasts the current findings with previous research, based on the experimental design and results.

claim: Observers may use statistical outliers within shapes (McCarthy and Warrington, 1986), or outliers relative to previously seen objects to identify distinctive parts.
source: We suggest that observers may use statistical outliers within shapes (McCarthy and Warrington, 1986), or outliers relative to previously seen objects to identify distinctive parts.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how distinctive parts are identified, with one citation.

claim: Observers agreed on the most distinctive parts of shapes and used this information as one of the main cues for category membership.
source: In summary, observers agreed on the most distinctive parts of shapes and used this information as one of the main cues for category membership.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by results from Experiments 5 and 6.

claim: When creating new shapes, distinctive parts were reproduced with modifications that retained their specific characteristics making them both distinctive and signifiers of their category.
source: In line with this, when creating new shapes, these distinctive parts were reproduced with modifications that retained their specific characteristics making them both distinctive and signifiers of their category.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by results from Experiments 4 and 5.

claim: Visual agnosia leads to profound deficits in object perception (McCarthy and Warrington, 1986; Riddoch and Humphreys, 1987; Goodale et al., 1991; Behrmann and Nishimura, 2010).
source: Yet disorders of object perception—such as visual agnosia (McCarthy and Warrington, 1986; Riddoch and Humphreys, 1987; Goodale et al., 1991; Behrmann and Nishimura, 2010) —lead to profound deficits.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical neuropsychology literature.

claim: Machine-learning systems typically require thousands of examples per category to rival human performance at recognizing objects in photographs (Huang et al., 2017; Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Szegedy et al., 2017; Szegedy et al., 2015; Szegedy et al., 2016; He et al., 2016; Radford, 2021; Kubilius et al., 2016; Jozwik et al., 2018; Jozwik et al., 2016; Jozwik et al., 2019).
source: Whereas machine-learning systems typically require thousands of examples per category to rival human performance at recognizing objects in photographs (Huang et al., 2017; Krizhevsky et al., 2012; Szegedy et al., 2017; Szegedy et al., 2015; Szegedy et al., 2016; He et al., 2016; Radford, 2021; Kubilius et al., 2016; Jozwik et al., 2018; Jozwik et al., 2016; Jozwik et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to machine learning literature.

claim: Human infants and adults appear to be able to generalize successfully from just a single example of a new category (Gelman and Markman, 1986; Gelman and Meyer, 2011; Gopnik and Sobel, 2000; Smith and Slone, 2017; Yuan et al., 2020; Gershkoff-Stowe et al., 1997; Landau et al., 1988; Landau et al., 1998; Pereira and Smith, 2009).
source: human infants and adults appear to be able to generalize successfully from just a single example of a new category (Gelman and Markman, 1986; Gelman and Meyer, 2011; Gopnik and Sobel, 2000; Smith and Slone, 2017; Yuan et al., 2020; Gershkoff-Stowe et al., 1997; Landau et al., 1988; Landau et al., 1998; Pereira and Smith, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to developmental and cognitive psychology research.

claim: One-shot categorization is a formally under-constrained inference problem (Feldman, 1992).
source: One-shot categorization is a formally under-constrained inference problem (Feldman, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Feldman's theoretical work.

claim: Humans seem to be able to draw consistent conclusions about category membership from sparse data (Feldman, 1992; Feldman, 1997).
source: It is thus remarkable that humans seem to be able to draw consistent conclusions about category membership from such sparse data (Feldman, 1992; Feldman, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Feldman's work.

claim: Human judgements about category membership presumably reflect assumptions about how—and by how much—objects within a category tend to differ from one another.
source: Their judgements presumably reflect assumptions about how—and by how much—objects within a category tend to differ from one another, which constrains the space of variants that are deemed likely.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the basis of human categorization judgements.

claim: Generative statistical models of shape play a key role in one-shot categorization.
source: We suggest that generative statistical models of shape play a key role in one-shot categorization.
evidence: This is the main theoretical claim of the paper, supported by the experimental findings.

claim: Most experimental studies on categorization use sets of pre-selected stimuli to define categories and discriminative tasks to test their hypotheses.
source: Most experimental studies on categorization use sets of pre-selected stimuli to define categories and discriminative tasks to test their hypotheses.
evidence: This describes typical methodology in the field based on review of literature.

claim: The main drawback of typical categorization approaches is that the assumed category-defining features are determined by the experimenter and might therefore differ from the features used in unrestricted categorization decisions.
source: The main drawback of this approach is that the assumed category-defining features are determined by the experimenter and might therefore differ from the features used in unrestricted categorization decisions.
evidence: This is a methodological critique based on logical reasoning.

claim: Discriminative tasks allow for simple strategies based on comparisons between objects, rather than probing the visual system's internal generative models.
source: Moreover, discriminative tasks allow for simple strategies based on comparisons between objects, rather than probing the visual system's internal generative models of objects which are thought to be central to how humans and machines can learn categories from sparse data (e.g., Fleming and Schmidt, 2019).
evidence: This is a methodological critique with citation to theoretical work.

claim: The resulting Variations are shaped by the features that participants consider important in the context of their previous experiences and by their internal visual imagery processes.
source: The resulting Variations are thus shaped by the features that participants consider important in the context of their previous experiences and by their internal visual imagery processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the drawing task reveals about cognitive processes.

claim: Different observers might in principle consider different features as significant so that across observers no coherent object categories would emerge.
source: In principle, different observers might consider different features as significant so that across observers no coherent object categories would emerge.
evidence: This is a logical possibility that the results argue against.

claim: There was a high degree of agreement between observers, suggesting general principles of how humans analyze single objects and extrapolate new category members from its features.
source: We found a high degree of agreement between observers, suggesting general principles of how humans analyze single objects and extrapolate new category members from its features.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by results across multiple experiments.

claim: Participants created Variations for different Exemplars varying in curvature characteristics and number of parts, resulting in a large dataset of over 1600 drawings.
source: Participants created Variations for different Exemplars varying in curvature characteristics and number of parts, resulting in a large dataset of over 1600 drawings, which were significantly more variable than mere copies of the Exemplars.
evidence: This describes the dataset created in Experiment 1.

claim: Despite the wide variety of Variations, the overwhelming majority of a representative subset of these shapes was correctly grouped with the originating Exemplar by independent observers.
source: Yet, despite the wide variety of Variations, the overwhelming majority of a representative subset of these shapes was correctly grouped with the originating Exemplar by independent observers, showing that our task yielded genuine distinct perceptual categories.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from Experiment 3.

claim: By asking participants to draw variants, the responses are necessarily limited by participant's skills with the digital drawing interface.
source: By asking participants to draw variants, the responses are necessarily limited by participant's skills with the digital drawing interface.
evidence: This is a limitation of the method acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Some people have lesser confidence or ability in drawing, and thus it is possible that some of drawings might not accurately reflect their mental image of a given variant.
source: Some people have lesser confidence or ability in drawing, and thus it is possible that some of drawings might not accurately reflect their mental image of a given variant.
evidence: This is a potential limitation of the drawing method.

claim: There was a substantial difference between copies (which were quite accurate) and variants (which were highly diverse).
source: It is also worth noting that there was a substantial difference between copies (which were quite accurate) and variants (which were highly diverse).
evidence: This observation from Experiment 2b addresses the limitation about drawing ability.

claim: Artistic ability did not prevent participants from depicting at least a subset of the varied and novel instances brought to mind by the exemplar.
source: This suggests that artistic ability did not prevent participants from depicting at least a subset of the varied and novel instances brought to mind by the exemplar.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the difference between copies and variants.

claim: Possible carry-over effects of Exemplars seen in previous trials might influence the drawings of later ones.
source: Another potential bias introduced by our approach is possible carry-over effects of Exemplars seen in previous trials influencing the drawings of later ones.
evidence: This is a potential limitation of the experimental design.

claim: The presence of distinctive features in some of the stimuli was the result of a decision by the experimenter, and it could be that such features occur less frequently in natural objects.
source: The presence of distinctive features in some of the stimuli (e.g., the 'twirl' in Exemplar 6) was therefore not accidental but the result of a decision by the experimenter, and it could be that such features occur less frequently in natural objects.
evidence: This is a limitation related to the hand-crafted nature of the stimuli.

claim: Even algorithmic stimulus generation does not fully solve the problem of experimenter control, as experimenters necessarily exert some degree of control over the kinds of stimuli through their decisions about the algorithm and training set.
source: However, even algorithmic stimulus generation does not fully solve the problem. Through their decisions about the algorithm and training set, experimenters necessarily exert some degree of control over the kinds of stimuli presented to participants, even if they do not hand-create or hand-select the individual instances, as we did.
evidence: This is a methodological argument about the inevitability of some experimenter influence.

claim: The finding that participants could consistently identify distinctive features without any explicit training suggests that both experimenter and participants shared assumptions about which features are important.
source: Despite our use of hand-drawn Exemplars, the finding that participants could consistently identify distinctive features without any explicit training—and treated these as defining class membership—suggests that both experimenter and participants shared assumptions about which features are important.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results that addresses the limitation about hand-crafted stimuli.

claim: The finding that participants created Variations that other participants recognized as belonging to the same class provides an existence proof for systematic generative processes.
source: More broadly, the finding that participants created Variations that other participants recognized as belonging to the same class provides an existence proof for systematic generative processes, irrespective of how frequently such distinctive features occur in natural objects.
evidence: This is a methodological argument about the validity of the findings despite limitations.

claim: Many variants appear to be related to the original Exemplar by a relatively straightforward (non-linear) spatial distortion operation that preserves the ordering of points, but alters their relative distances.
source: For example, we call one strategy 'Warping', as many variants appear to be related to the original Exemplar by a relatively straightforward (non-linear) spatial distortion operation that preserves the ordering of points, but alters their relative distances.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of one strategy used by participants, illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Through warping, a wide variety of shapes can be synthesized while largely retaining one-to-one correspondence with features of the prototype from which they are derived.
source: Through such warping, a wide variety of shapes can be synthesized while largely retaining one-to-one correspondence with features of the prototype from which they are derived.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the properties of the warping strategy.

claim: There is considerable evidence for perceptual organization processes that segment shapes into distinct subcomponents based on their geometrical properties (Hoffman and Richards, 1984; Hoffman and Singh, 1997; Siddiqi and Kimia, 1995; Biederman, 1987; Singh et al., 1999; Marr and Nishihara, 1978) and causal origin (Spröte et al., 2016).
source: There is considerable evidence for perceptual organization processes that segment shapes into distinct subcomponents based on their geometrical properties (Hoffman and Richards, 1984; Hoffman and Singh, 1997; Siddiqi and Kimia, 1995; Biederman, 1987; Singh et al., 1999; Marr and Nishihara, 1978) and causal origin (Spröte et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on shape perception.

claim: It seems intuitively plausible that parts might play a significant role in the generative process.
source: It thus seems intuitively plausible that parts might play a significant role in the generative process too.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on previous research and intuition.

claim: Even highly dissimilar shapes still shared 34% of their area with the originating Exemplar.
source: As a result, even highly dissimilar shapes still shared 34% of their area with the originating Exemplar (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1a right panel).
evidence: This is a result from Experiment 4 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Some parts were identified as being highly characteristic of the Exemplar's category and accordingly were varied in the Variations in ways to remain category defining.
source: Importantly, some parts were identified as being highly characteristic of the Exemplar's category and accordingly were varied in the Variations in ways to remain category defining (Experiment 6).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiments 5 and 6.

claim: The order of parts seems to have been retained in many Variations, showing that drawers relied on both individual parts as well as their relationships to create a new object.
source: In addition to reusing and changing individual parts, the order of parts also seems to have been retained in many Variations—showing that drawers relied on both individual parts as well as their relationships to create a new object.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the part order analysis from Experiment 4.

claim: Even shapes that appear to be created by a straightforward 'Warp' strategy are not inconsistent with a part-based analysis and recombination.
source: Indeed, even shapes that appear to be created by a straightforward 'Warp' strategy are not inconsistent with a part-based analysis and recombination.
evidence: This is an interpretation reconciling different apparent strategies.

claim: In Experiment 4, observers often (70% of trials) indicated only two or fewer corresponding parts.
source: One limitation of the analyses supporting these suggestions is that in Experiment 4, observers often (70% of trials) indicated only two or fewer corresponding parts.
evidence: This is a limitation of the part order analysis from Experiment 4.

claim: Participants often appear to have bundled together multiple elements into composite shape elements, effectively processing the parts in concert.
source: This was in part because participants often appear to have bundled together multiple elements—which a part-detection algorithm would treat as discrete—into composite shape elements, effectively processing the parts in concert.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why correspondence counts were low in Experiment 4.

claim: Although the drawings themselves were entirely unconstrained, Experiment 4 was explicitly focussed on corresponding parts by design, which only allows assessment of part-based strategies.
source: Moreover, although the drawings themselves were entirely unconstrained, it should be noted that Experiment 4 was explicitly focussed on corresponding parts by design, which only allows us to assess part-based strategies.
evidence: This is a limitation of what can be inferred from Experiment 4.

claim: Presumably it is necessary to retain certain statistical properties of the shape, such as the prevalence of sharp angles and straight edges, to maintain abstract concepts like 'spikiness'.
source: The exact nature of the features that define abstract concepts such as 'spikiness'—and thus allow observers to relate the Variations to the Exemplar—remain elusive. However, presumably it is necessary to retain certain statistical properties of the shape, such as the prevalence of sharp angles and straight edges.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about what features might define abstract shape properties.

claim: Eliminating core features—such as parts or straightness—was not a successful strategy for generating legal Variations.
source: Evidently, eliminating core features—such as parts or straightness—was not a successful strategy for generating legal Variations.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on examples shown in Figure 6.

claim: Observers analyze the Exemplar with respect to a number of features, ranging from basic properties like curvature to more high-level properties like 'spikiness', and then vary one or multiple of these features to create a new object.
source: Consequently, we suggest that observers analyze the Exemplar with respect to a number of features, ranging from basic properties like curvature to more high-level properties like 'spikiness', and then vary one or multiple of these features to create a new object.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the generative process based on the pattern of results.

claim: Perceived similarity between shapes can be predicted by considering a large number of shape features (Morgenstern et al., 2021).
source: This is consistent with recent work showing that perceived similarity between shapes can be predicted by considering a large number of shape features (Morgenstern et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: Observers seemed to share assumptions about the extent to which features could be varied while still retaining the categories' identity, as indicated by the small number of misclassifications in Experiment 3.
source: Yet, in general, observers seemed to share assumptions about the extent to which features could be varied while still retaining the categories' identity, as indicated by the small number of misclassifications in Experiment 3.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the high categorization accuracy in Experiment 3.

claim: These assumptions may be derived from the statistics of variations between items in the natural world.
source: It is interesting to speculate that these assumptions may therefore be derived from the statistics of variations between items in the natural world.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the origin of shared assumptions.

claim: Specific parts were reliably perceived as more distinctive than others and were the main catalyst driving categorization decisions, even if they comprised only a minority of the shapes' area.
source: Many of the generated shapes not only shared most of their parts, but, strikingly, specific parts were also reliably perceived as more distinctive than others and were the main catalyst driving categorization decisions, even if they comprised only a minority of the shapes' area.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiments 5 and 6.

claim: A crucial stage in one-shot categorization is the identification of those features within an object that are most likely to be 'distinctive' for defining the category.
source: This suggests that a crucial stage in one-shot categorization is the identification of those features within an object that are most likely to be 'distinctive' for defining the category.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the role of distinctive features.

claim: Observers' decisions about distinctive features are related to processes that identify signatures of the underlying generative processes responsible for creating the observed shape and which thus define the category.
source: We suggest that observers' decisions are related to processes that identify signatures of the underlying generative processes responsible for creating the observed shape and which thus define the category.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation linking distinctive features to generative processes.

claim: Statistical relations that are unlikely to occur under a random model (e.g., collinearity of features) are evidence of the operation of non-random generative processes.
source: This is closely related to Feldman's (Feldman, 1992; Feldman, 1997) theory of non-accidental features. Statistical relations that are unlikely to occur under a random model (e.g., collinearity of features) are evidence of the operation of non-random generative processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Feldman's theoretical work.

claim: Parts that have statistically distinct properties from the rest of the shape (Schmidt et al., 2019) or which are statistically distinct from parts of objects seen previously (Lake et al., 2015) are likely evidence of a category-defining process.
source: Similarly, parts that have statistically distinct properties from the rest of the shape (Schmidt et al., 2019)—or which are statistically distinct from parts of objects seen previously (Lake et al., 2015)—are likely evidence of a category-defining process.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: Parts that were deemed distinctive were also those that had the most significant effect on categorization (e.g., the 'twirl' feature in category 6).
source: Consistent with this idea, we find that parts that were deemed distinctive were also those that had the most significant effect of categorization (e.g., the 'twirl' feature in category 6; see Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a result from Experiments 5 and 6 shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Curvature characteristics (straight or curved lines) of Exemplars were preserved almost perfectly in most drawings, showing that these features were deemed non-random.
source: On a more global scale, curvature characteristics (straight or curved lines) of Exemplars were preserved almost perfectly in most drawings, showing that these features were also deemed non-random.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the curvature preservation finding from Figure 2b.

claim: Since the presented shapes were abstract, the part arrangement held no meaning and was therefore free to be modified, resulting in some Variations with changed part-ordering from the Exemplar.
source: Conversely, random features were altered more freely: Since the presented shapes were abstract, the part arrangement held no meaning and was therefore free to be modified (in contrast to familiar objects like a chair or a human), resulting in some Variations with changed part-ordering from the Exemplar.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the part order shuffling observed in Experiment 4.

claim: An important open question is which properties of parts or features are used to determine their status as outliers, and how these properties are determined, based on familiar objects and processing constraints of the visual system.
source: Yet an important open question is which properties of parts or features are used to determine their status as outliers, and how these properties are determined, based on familiar objects and processing constraints of the visual system.
evidence: This identifies a gap in understanding that remains to be addressed.

claim: Even though distinctiveness is an intuitive concept—as demonstrated by the high agreement by observers in Experiment 5—it is challenging to define it formally.
source: For example, even though distinctiveness is an intuitive concept—as demonstrated by the high agreement by observers in Experiment 5—it is challenging to define it formally.
evidence: This is an observation about the difficulty of formalizing the concept of distinctiveness despite empirical agreement.

claim: A large number of factors can affect the distinctiveness of a part or feature, ranging from purely geometric qualities to comparative analyses within the object or across other objects seen before.
source: A large number of factors can affect the distinctiveness of a part or feature, ranging from purely geometric qualities such as frequency of curvature changes (Baker et al., 2021; Attneave, 1957; e.g., a tentacle vs. a stub) to comparative analyses within the object (difference between part and other object parts) or across other objects seen before (difference between part and other objects' parts).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about factors that might determine distinctiveness, with some citations.

claim: Parts might be compared to an internal taxonomy of parts, each weighted with its probability of appearance, potentially informed by frequencies of parts in real-world objects or by their function (Mukherjee et al., 2019; Tversky, 1989).
source: More generally, parts might be compared to an internal taxonomy of parts, each weighted with its probability of appearance, potentially informed by frequencies of parts in real-world objects or by their function (Mukherjee et al., 2019; Tversky, 1989).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about how parts might be represented, with citations.

claim: Another important open question is how parts are parameterized so that identity-preserving variations can be generated.
source: Another important open question is how parts are parameterized so that identity-preserving variations can be generated.
evidence: This identifies another gap in understanding.

claim: Skeletal representations offer a promising avenue for potential representations (Destler et al., 2019; Wilder et al., 2011; Wilder et al., 2018; Wilder et al., 2019).
source: Skeletal representations (e.g., Feldman and Singh, 2006) offer a promising avenue for potential representations (Destler et al., 2019; Wilder et al., 2011; Wilder et al., 2018; Wilder et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about promising approaches, supported by citations.

claim: Humans are not merely passive observers, who assign objects to categories based on their relative similarities in a fixed feature space.
source: Taken together, the results of our experiments suggest that humans are not merely passive observers, who assign objects to categories based on their relative similarities in a fixed feature space.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: A key aspect of human generalization is our ability to identify important signatures of generative processes and then to run internal routines that actively synthesize new objects that we have never actually observed.
source: Instead, a key aspect of human generalization is our ability to identify important signatures of generative processes and then to run internal routines that actively synthesize new objects that we have never actually observed.
evidence: This is the main theoretical conclusion of the paper, supported by the experimental findings.

claim: Drawing tasks present experimenters with challenges, particularly in terms of analyzing the resulting drawings.
source: Thus, although drawing tasks present experimenters with challenges—particularly in terms of analyzing the resulting drawings—they also provide a promising avenue into research not only about object categorization but also human creativity.
evidence: This is an observation about the methodological challenges and opportunities of drawing tasks.

claim: There is a notable difference between participants as to how much they tended to deviate from the Exemplars, raising the question of what drives these individual differences.
source: As seen in Figure 1d, there is a notable difference between participants as to how much they tended to deviate from the Exemplars, raising the question of what drives these individual differences.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 1d that raises a question for future research.

claim: The fact that observers can derive diverse but constrained variations from a single exemplar suggests a deep perceptual understanding about the ways things in the natural world tend to vary.
source: The fact that observers can derive diverse but constrained variations from a single exemplar suggests a deep perceptual understanding about the ways things in the natural world tend to vary.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the main findings.

claim: In future work, it would be interesting to analyze the similarities between human drawings using artificial neural networks trained on datasets of line drawings, such as the 'Quick Draw!' dataset (Jongejan et al., 2016; Ha and Eck, 2017; Xu et al., 2021; Kabakus, 2020).
source: In future work, it would also be interesting to analyze the similarities between human drawings (and their similarities to the exemplars) using artificial neural networks trained on datasets of line drawings, such as the 'Quick Draw!' dataset (Jongejan et al., 2016; Ha and Eck, 2017; Xu et al., 2021; Kabakus, 2020).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research with citations.

claim: Each of the human drawings could be fed into a neural network, and a feature vector describing the shape derived, allowing an automated quantitative similarity analysis to be performed.
source: In particular, each of the human drawings (or exemplars) could be fed into such a network, and a feature vector describing the shape derived, allowing an automated quantitative similarity analysis to be performed.
evidence: This is a methodological suggestion for future research.

claim: Training a neural network model to reproduce the types of generalizations that humans produce when presented with a single exemplar would answer questions about whether exposure to human-created line drawings is necessary to generalize like humans.
source: Even more intriguing is the possibility of training a neural network model to reproduce the types of generalizations that humans produce when presented with a single exemplar. This would answer questions, such as whether it is necessary to be exposed to human-created line drawings in order to generalize like humans, or whether a visual diet consisting entirely of natural images is sufficient.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research that would address theoretical questions.

claim: Training a neural network to reproduce human generalizations would allow a more rigorous test of whether part-based representations are necessary to capture the full range of human generalization.
source: It would also allow a more rigorous test of whether part-based representations are necessary to capture the full range of human generalization.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research that would test theoretical claims.

claim: One-shot generalization as exhibited by human observers remains a significant challenge for artificial vision systems.
source: However, to date, one-shot generalization as exhibited by our observers remains a significant challenge for artificial vision systems.
evidence: This is a claim about the current state of artificial intelligence.

claim: The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee of the Department of Psychology and Sports Sciences of the Justus-Liebig University Giessen (LEK-FB06; protocol code 2016-0007, approved 18 April 2016).
source: The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Ethics Committee of the Department of Psychology and Sports Sciences of the Justus-Liebig University Giessen (LEK-FB06; protocol code 2016-0007, approved 18 April 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the research.
